blocks.text: **Microsoft Excel** is spreadsheet software from Microsoft. It organises data, performs calculations, analyses information and creates charts.

blocks.title: Building blocks
rows: An Excel file that contains sheets.
A grid of rows, columns and cells.
The **intersection of a row and a column** - the basic data-entry unit.

blocks.title: A1 notation
items: In A1 notation the **column comes before the row**.
**A1** is the first cell; **A25** means column A, row 25.
The 19th column is **S**, so row 13, column 19 is **S13**.

blocks.title: Default names
items: A new, unsaved English desktop workbook is normally **Book1**; further new workbooks are Book2, Book3...
A sheet is normally named **Sheet1** (then Sheet2, Sheet3...).
**Book1** is a workbook name; **Sheet1** is a worksheet name (workbook contains sheets; worksheet contains cells).

blocks.title: Spreadsheet history
items: VisiCalc
Widely recognised as the **first personal-computer spreadsheet**
Lotus 1-2-3
A prominent **DOS-based** spreadsheet
**Microsoft Excel** first released for the **Macintosh**
The **Windows** edition of Excel followed

blocks.text: Excel was developed by Microsoft, including its first Macintosh release. The claim 'Excel is written in C++' is an oversimplification across versions and components, so do not treat it as a firm fact.
LibreOffice and Apache OpenOffice are **separate suites**, even though both name their spreadsheet Calc.

blocks.title: Name Box vs Formula Bar
blocks.text: The **Name Box** shows the address (for example C7). The **Formula Bar** shows the contents (for example =SUM(F2:F9)). The cell itself normally displays the calculated result. **Ctrl + F1** expands or collapses the Ribbon. Available tabs vary with version and selected objects.

items: **.xlsx** cannot retain VBA macro code.
Lotus 1-2-3 used **.123, .wk1, .wk3, .wk4 and .wks** across its releases. An extension question that offers both .123 and .wk1 is ambiguous.

blocks.text: Users can change the starting number of sheets or use templates.
A legacy .xls file keeps the older, smaller worksheet limits.

blocks.title: Important capacities
rows: Limited only by available memory and resources

blocks.text: 255 is the **maximum** column width - not the default width and not the cell text limit (that is 32,767). 'Unlimited' sheets is not literally true: it depends on resources. 341 functions is a legacy figure, not a universal cap, because available functions vary by version and platform.

blocks.text: Rows = 1,048,576 | Columns = 16,384 | Cell text = 32,767 | Width = 255 | Height = 409.

blocks.title: Three ways to edit cell content
items: Select the cell and press **F2**.
Or double-click the cell, when direct in-cell editing is enabled.
Or edit through the **Formula Bar**.

blocks.text: **F11** uses the **default chart type**, not specifically a bar chart. **Alt** alone only activates the Ribbon access keys - it does not edit a cell.
Deleted something by accident? Use Undo: **Ctrl + Z**. Keyboard layout, version and laptop Fn settings can affect shortcuts.

blocks.title: Select and move
rows: Expand the selection towards the whole worksheet
Beginning of the worksheet, normally A1
Last cell of the **used range** (not the final possible cell)

items: Inside a data region, repeated presses of Ctrl + Shift + Spacebar may be needed.
Hold **Ctrl** while clicking to select non-adjacent cells or ranges.
For date and time together: **Ctrl + ;**, then a space, then **Ctrl + Shift + ;**.
On a US keyboard the time shortcut is also written Ctrl + Shift + :.
Number formatting determines what is displayed for a date or time.

blocks.title: Date display and alignment
rows: On a US keyboard applies a day-month-year style **date format** (often written Ctrl + Shift + #). It only formats - it does not insert today's date.
Under General alignment, recognised dates and times align **right** because they are numeric.
Manual formatting can override alignment, and a date-like entry stored as text may behave differently.

blocks.text: TODAY = date | NOW = date and time | Shortcut entry = fixed value | Function result = recalculated.

Cells can contain numbers, text, logical values, errors and formulas. A formula calculates a numeric, text, logical or error result. Formatting generally changes how a value looks, not the number actually stored.

blocks.title: Number formats
rows: Numeric values shown with currency symbols
A numeric serial displayed as a calendar date
A fraction of a day displayed as time
Treats entries as text; useful for identifiers with leading zeros

blocks.text: 'Character' is not a separate introductory entry category in Excel, although characters can be entered as text.

blocks.title: AutoFill and Transpose
rows: Copies entries/formulas or extends patterns (number sequences, dates, weekdays, month names) using the **fill handle**.
Changes **rows into columns** and columns into rows.
Use **Paste Special > Transpose** or the **TRANSPOSE** function.

blocks.title: Freeze Panes and Split
items: **Freeze Panes** keeps headings visible while scrolling. **View > Freeze Panes** offers Top Row, First Column and Freeze Panes.
Select **B2** and freeze: row 1 and column A remain visible.
Freezing controls the view - it does **not** protect cells from editing.
**Split** divides the same worksheet into separately scrollable panes; the selection can produce two or four panes.
Modern route: **View > Window group > Split**. Older Excel 2003 route: Window > Split.

blocks.title: Merge cells
rows: Combines adjacent cells into one larger cell.
In left-to-right sheets only the **upper-left** content is kept; other contents are discarded after confirmation.
Merging does **not** join the text of every cell together.

blocks.title: ##### display
rows: The column is **too narrow** for a formatted number or date.
A negative date/time result can also show #####.
Widen or AutoFit the column, reduce decimals, or use a shorter format.
The displayed hashes do not automatically mean data was lost.

blocks.title: Paste Special options

blocks.text: All of these are Paste Special capabilities - Values is **not** its only purpose.

blocks.title: Comments and Notes
items: Traditional comments are called **Notes** in Microsoft 365.
Modern **Comments** support **threaded discussions**.
A red triangle at a cell's upper-right corner traditionally indicated a comment; in modern Excel it indicates a **Note**.
'Cell tip' is an informal term found in older exam material.

blocks.title: CSV - Comma-Separated Values
rows: Plain-text tabular data: records on separate lines, fields commonly separated by commas (for example 'Name,Marks' then 'Asha,85').
Normally saves the **active sheet's** displayed text/values.
It does **not** preserve workbook formatting, charts or multiple sheets.

blocks.title: Excel for the web and HTML
items: **Excel for the web** is the browser-based edition; a free personal version is available with a Microsoft account.
It supports common formulas, formatting and collaboration, but desktop capabilities differ.
**Internet Assistant Wizard** is a historical HTML-conversion tool.
Supported desktop versions can use **File > Save As > Web Page (.htm/.html)**. Keep the original workbook because HTML may lose Excel features.

blocks.title: Word-Excel integration (OLE)
rows: Word is the **container/client**; Excel is the **supplying server**.
Depend on which application contains the object.

blocks.text: The **$** fixes the part immediately after it. It does **not** protect the cell. While editing a formula reference, **F4** cycles through the reference forms.

blocks.title: Copy two columns right and two rows down
Exam examples
items: **$A$9** and **$A$5** are absolute references.
**A$9** is mixed: row 9 is fixed. **$A4** is mixed: column A is fixed.
Copy $A4 one row down: **$A5**. Copy $A4 one column right: **$A4** (unchanged).
Second row, seventh column is **G2**; its absolute form is **$G$2**.

blocks.title: Cross-sheet references
rows: Quotes are needed around a sheet name that contains a space.
Separates the sheet name from the cell reference.

blocks.title: Range notation
items: A **colon** joins the first and last cells of a range.
**B1:G10** covers columns B to G and rows 1 to 10. **B1:E5** is the inclusive rectangle from B1 through E5.
**$B$2:$B$10** is an absolute range.
**A9:E9** contains 5 cells. **A9:A99** contains 99 - 9 + 1 = **91** cells.

blocks.title: Counting cells in a rectangle (columns x rows)

blocks.text: The formula **=ROWS(A1:D7)*COLUMNS(A1:D7)** returns 28. Note that =COUNT(A1:D7) gives 28 only if all 28 cells contain numbers - COUNT counts numeric entries, not automatically all cells.

items: COUNTA also includes formulas that return an empty string ""; COUNTBLANK counts those as blank too.

rows: 3 (all three zeros count; the text 'a' is ignored)

blocks.title: VLOOKUP - vertical lookup
rows: Searches the **first column** of a table and returns a value from a specified column in the matching row.
The table's **third column** supplies the result.

blocks.title: IF and concatenation
rows: Tests a condition and selects between two results.
=IF(B2>=40,"Pass","Fail") shows Pass when B2 is 40 or more, otherwise Fail.
=A1&" "&B1 joins two cell values with a space between them.

rows: Any sequence of characters, including none
*Pen* matches Pen, Pencil, Gel Pen, etc.
P?n matches Pen or Pcn, but not Pencil

blocks.text: COUNTIF counts **matching cells**, not the quantities in the Qty column.

blocks.title: Formula essentials
items: Standard formulas begin with **=**. A **function** is a predefined calculation, such as SUM.
With A1 to A4 holding 10, 20, 30, 40: =SUM(A1:A4), =A1+A2+A3+A4 and =SUM(A1,A2,A3,A4) all return **100**.
There is **no** standard SUBTRACT worksheet function - use the minus sign. =20-8 returns 12 and =A1-B1 subtracts B1 from A1.
A formula shown in the Formula Bar can produce a different displayed result in the cell.

blocks.title: Order of operations
items: Parentheses control the order; multiplication/division come before addition/subtraction.
Consecutive divisions run **left to right**.
**TRUE = 1** and **FALSE = 0** when typed directly as SUM arguments.
SUM normally **ignores logical values** in referenced cells or ranges (so a row holding TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE adds up to 0).

sections.title: FLOOR, CEILING, SUMSQ, FACT, MOD, ODD and EVEN

blocks.title: Syntax and meaning
rows: For positive significance, rounds to the nearest multiple **at or below** the number.
For positive numbers and significance, rounds to the nearest multiple **at or above** the number.
Factorial: multiplies the positive integers from 1 to n. **0! is defined as 1**.
The **remainder** after division. A zero divisor gives #DIV/0!.
Rounds **away from zero** to an odd integer.
Rounds **away from zero** to an even integer.

items: Exact multiples stay unchanged: FLOOR(25,5) = CEILING(25,5) = 25.
=FLOOR(-54/10,1) = **-6**: with positive significance, negative numbers round down, away from zero.
Traditional FLOOR and CEILING **require** the significance argument. The standard function is **CEILING**, not CEIL.

rows: Next odd integer away from zero

blocks.text: An integer that already has the required parity stays unchanged (EVEN(40) = 40). Factorial, remainder and parity-rounding solve different tasks - read the function name before calculating.

blocks.title: Using Goal Seek (route: Data > What-If Analysis > Goal Seek)
items: **Set cell** - choose the cell that holds the formula (for example Revenue).
**To value** - type the result you want (for example 2,000).
**By changing cell** - choose the single input to adjust (for example Quantity).
Example: with Price $20 and Quantity 100, Revenue is $2,000; Goal Seek finds the sales quantity needed for a revenue target at a fixed price.

blocks.text: Pie = one series | Sparkline = in-cell chart | Goal Seek = target result to required input.

revision: Workbook contains sheets; worksheet contains cells. A new workbook is Book1 and a sheet is Sheet1; the column comes before the row in A1 notation (row 13, column 19 = S13).
Excel first released for Macintosh in 1985 and for Windows in 1987; VisiCalc was the first PC spreadsheet and Lotus 1-2-3 a DOS spreadsheet.
Name Box = cell address; Formula Bar = contents. The cell shows the calculated result. Ctrl + F1 expands or collapses the Ribbon.
.xls = legacy (97-2003); .xlsx = standard since 2007; .xlsm = macro-enabled; .xltm = macro-enabled template; .xlsx cannot keep VBA code.
Default sheets: 3 in Excel 2003/2007/2010 and 1 from Excel 2013 onward.
Excel 2003: 65,536 rows x 256 columns (last column IV). Excel 2007+: 1,048,576 rows x 16,384 columns (last column XFD).
Capacities: 32,767 characters per cell, column width 255, row height 409 points, zoom 10% - 400%.
Ctrl+N new, Ctrl+O open, F12 Save As, Ctrl+W close, Shift+F11 new sheet, F2 edit cell, Alt+Enter new line in a cell, Alt+= AutoSum, F11 chart sheet, Alt+F11 VBA editor.
Shift+Space selects a row; Ctrl+Space selects a column; Ctrl+9 hides rows, Ctrl+0 hides columns; Ctrl+End goes to the last used cell.
=TODAY() and =NOW() recalculate; Ctrl+; and Ctrl+Shift+; insert fixed date and time values.
Reference types: A1 relative, $A$1 absolute, $A1 and A$1 mixed; F4 cycles them. Copying A1 two columns right and two rows down gives C3.
COUNT = numbers, COUNTA = non-empty, COUNTBLANK = empty, COUNTIF = one condition, COUNTIFS = many conditions; COUNTNUMBERS does not exist.
Wildcards: * any characters, ? one character, ~ escapes a wildcard. VLOOKUP's FALSE means exact match.
Charts: column compares categories, line shows trends, pie shows one series. Sparklines are in-cell charts (Line, Column, Win/Loss); Goal Seek finds an input for a target result.
